## The afterlife

On 17 July 2014, at the annual DC Loves Dilla concert, his mother announced that she was giving his equipment to the Smithsonian. The National Museum of African American History and Culture accessioned the MPC3000 Limited Edition, its gold plaque reading edition number 0449, and the Minimoog Voyager, serial 263, along with the power cord, a cable and the factory case. Both are in the museum's Musical Crossroads exhibition. She had refused at first. The curator, Timothy Anne Burnside, spent years talking her round.

That is an unusual destination for a drum machine, and it is the clearest institutional statement of what he is understood to have done: the objects are there as instruments of American music history, in the same building as the rest of it.

The estate took longer and went worse. He signed a will in September 2005 naming his mother, his two daughters and his brother, with an accountant as executor. In 2008 an unfinished album leaked and the family's objections played out in public, including a full-page advertisement in Billboard. The executor resigned in 2009 after the family challenged the administration, and control passed through another administrator before his mother and his brother Illa J finally held it themselves. She has spent two decades doing that work in public, and has said she spent years unable to draw anything from his catalog at all.

The critical apparatus arrived late but solidly. Dan Charnas's biography, published in 2022, reframed him as a rhythmic innovator rather than a cult producer, was reviewed everywhere from the New York Times to the LA Times, and won a PEN award the following year. Charnas teaches a course on him at New York University. There have been museum exhibitions at Wayne State, The Broad and Guild Hall. In 2024 Detroit's city council passed a resolution honoring him, sponsored by its president, and the city named a street after him near the house he grew up in.

the drum programming behind it is a set of things you can actually do, collected in [how to make Dilla type beats](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-dilla-type-beats/)

## Questions people ask

### What was the cause of J Dilla's death?

He died at home in Los Angeles on 10 February 2006, at thirty-two, three days after Donuts was released on his birthday. The cause given at the time was cardiac arrest, stated by his mother, after years of complications and a recent hospitalization for pneumonia. No autopsy has ever been reported.

### What illness did J Dilla have?

In January 2002 he collapsed and was found to have a platelet count under 10, against a normal range of 140 to 180. A specialist diagnosed thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, a rare blood disorder, and told him there was no cure. A lupus diagnosis came later, in 2005, and the reporting closest to the family hedged it even then. The complications, not the labels, are what disabled him: kidney failure, dialysis three times a week, and the loss of half his body weight.

### Why is J Dilla considered so important?

Because he built a third way of feeling time and then proved it on records other people paid for. Before him, American popular music had straight time and swung time. He ran both at once, by giving each voice in a drum pattern its own timing, and the result was strange enough that musicians spent the next twenty years learning to play it on acoustic instruments.

### What is special about Dilla's drums?

Each voice sits in a consistent place that is not the grid, and the voices disagree with each other. Because it is sequenced rather than played, the same disagreement repeats identically in every bar, so the ear learns it as a groove instead of hearing it as a mistake. There is no single offset: measurements of different records find early snares, late hats, straight hats and dragging claps, depending on the record.

### How do you make beats like J Dilla?

Give the parts different timing instead of nudging the whole pattern. Set the hats to one swing value and the snare to another, or quantize one voice and play another by hand, then leave it alone so the displacement repeats. Choose samples that were played loosely to begin with. And start the loop somewhere other than the kick. Our guides to [boom bap drums](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-boom-bap-drums/) and [chopping a drum break](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-chop-a-drum-break/) cover the mechanics.

### What equipment did J Dilla use?

By his own account: an SP-12, then an SP-1200, then an MPC60 and its successor, then the MPC3000, which he stayed on. He also had an Akai S950 early, a Minimoog Voyager from 2002, and a BOSS SP-303 in his last year. The MPC3000 Limited Edition and the Voyager are both in the Smithsonian.

### What was J Dilla's real name?

James Dewitt Yancey. He recorded as Jay Dee for most of his career and changed it to J Dilla around 2001, to stop being confused with the producer Jermaine Dupri.

The house in Conant Gardens ran on shifts so the basement could keep working. Twenty-odd years after it stopped, drummers in conservatories are being taught to play what came out of it.

# Kenny Segal

> How Kenny Segal makes records: live players over samples, the SP-404 used as an effects box, drums edited hit by hit, and sampling the spaces between the notes.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/kenny-segal/  
Published 2026-09-20, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries.

---

Most producers who get called an SP-404 user are describing a sampler. In this case the machine is closer to a pedalboard: live drums, played in a room, running out through a cheap box of effects and back in again, until the recording stops sounding like a recording.

Kenny Segal is a Los Angeles producer best known for his records with billy woods — Hiding Places in 2019 and Maps in 2023 — and for work with R.A.P. Ferreira, Armand Hammer, Open Mike Eagle and Busdriver. His method is built around live musicians playing over samples, and the SP-404 sits in that chain as a processor rather than as the thing the beat is made on. His own description: start with the sample, get a vibe, then have people come and play on top of it.

## The short version

- **Known for**: Hiding Places (2019), Maps (2023) with billy woods

- **Studio**: a home room in Jefferson Park, Los Angeles

- **Samplers**: reported as a cache of SP-404s

- **Plays**: Omnichord and a Bastl MicroGranny on record

- **Method**: sample first, then live players over it

- **Signature**: sampling the spaces between the notes

## The 404 as an effects unit

The clearest public document of how he uses the machine is a sample pack he put out in 2017, because one of its folders is labeled for exactly what it contains: live drums processed through SP-404 effects. Not drums sequenced on a 404. Drums played, recorded, and then run through the box for what it does to them.

The same pack includes a circuit-bent Omnichord, a hacked toy sampler, and a folder of vinyl noise, tape hiss and field recordings. That is a fair picture of the palette: acoustic sources and broken electronics, with a cheap sampler's effects as the glue. If you want to know what the 404's ancestors did to audio in that role, our piece on [the SP-303](https://gazillionindustries.com/sp-303/) covers it, and [the SP-404 story](https://gazillionindustries.com/sp-404-history/) covers how the line got there.

## Sampling the spaces between the notes

That phrase is his, and it is the most useful idea in his published method. Ableton put out a breakdown of his approach in 2017 with a downloadable session, and the structure is revealing: each drum element sits on its own arrangement track rather than in a clip, so that any individual hit can be muted, reversed or pitched on its own.

What that gives you is not a loop with variations. It is a performance you can edit at the level of the single hit, which is why his drums breathe in a way programmed drums usually do not and why they never quite repeat. The spaces are the material: the bar of room tone between two phrases, the breath before a horn line, the decay nobody else kept.

[Gazillion Industries](https://gazillionindustries.com/) makes plugins for records built this way, where the room and the noise are the content rather than the problem.

## The room, from the people in it

Musicians who have recorded there describe a Rhodes, a Casio CZ-101, a polyphonic Moog, a spread of pedals, and a microphone and preamp collection good enough that one of them singled out how clear the drums came back. They also describe him working the controls during takes rather than afterward, which fits everything else about the method: the processing is part of the performance, not a stage that happens later.

Small practical detail worth stealing: on at least one record the guitars went straight in, with no amplifier. A guitar direct into a chain of samplers and pedals is a different instrument from a guitar in front of a speaker, and on the right record it is the better one.

## Why the records sound like that

Hiding Places and Maps are rap records where the instrumental rarely behaves like a beat. The loops drift, the drums arrive late or not at all, and there are long passages where what is holding time is a musician rather than a grid. That is a direct consequence of the working order: if the sample comes first and the players come second, what you end up with is a performance of a loop rather than a loop with performances on top.

It is also the opposite of the dominant approach, where the grid is fixed first and everything is fitted to it. Both produce good records. They produce different kinds.

## Questions people ask

### What does Kenny Segal use?

A home studio in Los Angeles with a reported cache of SP-404s, a Rhodes, a Casio CZ-101, a polyphonic Moog, pedals, and a good microphone and preamp collection. He plays Omnichord and a Bastl MicroGranny on record.

### How does he use the SP-404?

Mostly as an effects processor on material played live, rather than as the sequencer. His own sample pack documents live drums run through the machine's effects.

### What is his production process?

In his words: start with the sample, get a vibe, then bring musicians in to play over it. The drums are then edited at the level of individual hits, each on its own track.

### What records should I start with?

Hiding Places with billy woods (2019) and Maps (2023). Then the work with R.A.P. Ferreira, Armand Hammer and Open Mike Eagle.

The drum bus end of it, in one control.

We make [DRUGS](https://gazillionindustries.com/drugs.html). The drum bus end of it, in one control.

## What to take from it

Two things. Put the processor in the performance rather than after it: if a cheap sampler's effects are going to be on the drums, run the drums through them while people are playing and commit. And treat every hit as editable rather than every bar: a kit on separate tracks, where one snare can be reversed or dropped, is a different instrument from a loop.

The machine everyone associates with him was never really the point. The players in the room were.

# Madlib

> How Madlib actually works: the hotel-room rig behind Madvillainy, sampling whole records, ten minutes a beat, and how the Quasimoto voice is really made.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/madlib/  
Published 2026-09-20, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries.

---

A producer checks into a hotel in São Paulo in 2002 with a portable turntable, a cheap sampler and a tape deck, and comes home with the beats for a record people are still arguing about. His summary of the gear conversation: people think they need all this equipment.

Otis Jackson Jr., who records as Madlib, was born in 1973 in Oxnard, California, into a musical family, and has been the most prolific producer in independent hip hop for twenty-five years. His method is unusual in two ways: he samples whole records rather than hunting for one break, and he refuses to spend long on a beat. "I don't like to spend more than 10 minutes at a time on a beat," he has said. "I'm not like Dre; I don't take a week on a snare."

## The short version

- **Born**: 1973, Oxnard, California

- **Family**: father a musician, brother Oh No, uncle Jon Faddis

- **Key records**: Madvillainy, Champion Sound, Shades of Blue, Piñata, Bandana

- **Rig, famously**: portable turntable, an SP-303, a tape deck

- **Pace**: ten minutes a beat, and hundreds never kept

- **Mixdown**: straight to two channels, no stems

## The hotel room

In late 2002 he went to Brazil for a Red Bull Music Academy session and took almost nothing with him. The tracks he made there fed into Madvillainy, released in 2004 with MF DOOM, and his own account of the setup is specific: a portable turntable, a BOSS SP-303 and a little tape deck. He has repeated the point every time anybody asks about equipment.

That is not a story about minimalism as a virtue. It is a story about what a sampler is for. If your method is to find something in a record and get it into a loop quickly, the smallest box that can do that is the correct box, and everything else is a delay between hearing the thing and having it. Our piece on [the SP-303](https://gazillionindustries.com/sp-303/) covers what that particular machine did to whatever went through it.

## The whole record

Most sampling producers are looking for a break: one bar, one phrase, one chord. Madlib's description of his own practice is the opposite. "Every time I sample a record, I do the whole record," he has said — meaning he works through an entire album while it is in front of him, making beats out of everything usable rather than extracting one part.

The output of that method is volume, and volume is the point. Series like the Beat Konducta and the Medicine Show exist because the beats exist; they are published quantities of a process that never stops. His engineer's account is that hundreds of pieces get made and simply erased by the evening.

## Two channels, no stems

He mixes to stereo as he goes. "I'd lay the beat straight out. To two channels." There are no session files with thirty tracks waiting to be balanced later, which means every decision is committed at the moment it is made and cannot be revisited.

That creates a real engineering problem downstream, and there is a documented solution to it. Dave Cooley, the engineer who mixed and mastered a lot of this material, has described manufacturing stereo width out of Madlib's mono loops using gates, reverb and a signal generator — building a stereo field after the fact because the source did not have one. That is the cost of committing early, and someone has to pay it.

[Gazillion Industries](https://gazillionindustries.com/) builds plugins for this end of the process: commit, print, move on.

## The Quasimoto voice

The high-pitched character on his own records is not a pitch shifter. His explanation, given in several interviews over several years, is mechanical: he slows the tape down and raps slowly against it, so that at normal speed the voice comes back fast and high. The formants move with the pitch because the whole recording moved, which is why it sounds like a different creature rather than a processed human. See [formant shifting](https://gazillionindustries.com/formant-shifting/) for why that distinction matters and [varispeed](https://gazillionindustries.com/what-is-varispeed/) for the mechanism.

## The caveman and the iPad

In 2002 he said, "I don't use computers. I'm a caveman." By 2019 he was saying he made all of the beats for Bandana, his second album with Freddie Gibbs, on an iPad.

Both statements are true and the change is smaller than it looks. An iPad running a sampler app is the same object as a portable turntable and an SP-303: the smallest box that gets from hearing something to having it in a loop. The tool changed and the method did not.

## The catalog, briefly

Lootpack got him onto Stones Throw. Quasimoto gave him a voice to rap in. Yesterdays New Quintet let him play every instrument on a jazz record under invented band names. Shades of Blue gave him the Blue Note archive to rebuild. Champion Sound with [J Dilla](https://gazillionindustries.com/j-dilla/) in 2003 put two producers over each other's beats. Madvillainy with [MF DOOM](https://gazillionindustries.com/mf-doom/) in 2004 is the one most people start with. Piñata in 2014 and Bandana in 2019 with Freddie Gibbs proved the method still worked on records that needed to sell. Sound Ancestors in 2021, assembled with Kieran Hebden, is the closest thing to an edited overview of what he does.

The working method, as things you can do rather than things to admire, is in [how to make Madlib type beats](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-madlib-type-beats/).

## Questions people ask

### What equipment does Madlib use?

Famously a portable turntable, a BOSS SP-303 and a tape deck on the trip that produced Madvillainy material; samplers and turntables generally; and more recently an iPad, on which he says he made all the beats for Bandana.

### How does Madlib make the Quasimoto voice?

He slows the tape down and raps slowly, so the vocal plays back fast and high. He has said repeatedly that he does not pitch-shift the voice.

### How fast does Madlib work?

By his own account, about ten minutes on a beat before moving on, and he samples a whole record at a time rather than looking for one break. Most of what he makes is never released.

### How many records does Madlib own?

Nobody has published a number, including him. His own answers have ranged from a couple of rooms to four rooms and a wish for ten. Any specific figure you see is somebody's estimate.

The bus compressor we make for exactly this material — breaks that arrived already dusty.

We make [DRUGS](https://gazillionindustries.com/drugs.html). The bus compressor we make for exactly this material — breaks that arrived already dusty.

## What to take from it

The transferable part is not the gear list. It is the refusal to treat a beat as precious: ten minutes, commit it to two channels, and go to the next one, which over twenty years produces a catalog nobody can survey. Most producers' problem is not that they lack tools. It is that they spend four hours on a snare and end the year with nine beats.

A hotel room, three objects, and a record people are still taking apart. The gear was never the variable.

# MF DOOM

> Who MF DOOM was and how he actually made beats: the birth date everyone had wrong, the loop-drums-808 method in his own words, the machines, and the imposter shows.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/mf-doom/  
Published 2026-09-20, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries.

---

A rapper whose group was dropped the week his brother died, who disappeared for most of a decade, and who came back in a metal mask so nobody would have to look at the person underneath. Then he made the beats too.

Daniel Dumile, who recorded as MF DOOM, was born on 13 July 1971 in London and raised in Long Beach, New York. He produced most of his own records and a great many for other people under the name Metal Fingers, working from an MPC-2000XL and a hardware multitracker, with a method he described plainly: find the loop, put drums on it, polish it with an 808, and leave it close to the original. He died on 31 October 2020. His family announced it on 31 December.

## The short version

- **Born**: 13 July 1971, London; died 31 October 2020

- **First act**: KMD, with his brother DJ Subroc

- **Rebirth**: Operation: Doomsday, 19 October 1999

- **Aliases**: King Geedorah, Viktor Vaughn, Metal Fingers

- **Machines**: MPC-2000XL, a Roland VS multitracker, a Casio FZ sampler

- **Method**: loop, drums, 808, stop

## The date almost everyone had wrong

For twenty years the internet celebrated his birthday on 9 January. It was wrong. Court records give 13 July 1971, and the friend who ran his reissue label has said they wished each other happy birthday in July. Okayplayer, which had published the January date for years, retracted it publicly. It is a small thing and it is also a good indicator of how much of what circulates about him is repetition rather than reporting.

The same applies to Operation: Doomsday. The anniversary gets marked on 20 April every year. The record came out on 19 October 1999, which is documented by the invoice, posted publicly by the man who released it, and Genius appended a correction to its own article saying so.

## KMD, and the years out of sight

He started as Zev Love X in KMD with his younger brother, DJ Subroc. In 1993 Subroc was killed, and the group's second album was shelved by its label. What followed was years out of the industry, and he has spoken about that period only obliquely. The Casio FZ sampler he kept hold of through it turns up in accounts of the work he made afterward, which tells you something about what he was prioritizing.

The mask arrived with the return. It is worth noticing what it actually accomplished: it made the records about the writing and the beats, and it made the performer interchangeable, which is a decision with consequences we will get to.

## How the beats were made

The clearest statement he gave about his production method came at a Red Bull Music Academy lecture in 2011, asked how he built one of his best-known tracks: "I heard the loop first, caught the loop, put the drums to it, polished it up with the 808. I don't really overdo it too much. I like to keep it as close to the original as possible, leave something to the imagination, but enough to get the translation across. Then just write to it. Keep it simple."

That is a complete production philosophy in four sentences, and it is the opposite of the chop-everything-into-fragments approach of his most famous collaborator. DOOM found a loop that already worked and stayed out of its way.

Operation: Doomsday itself was made on borrowed equipment. The DJ Stretch Armstrong has described it being cut in about three weeks in his apartment, on his sampler, off his records. Later he worked on an MPC-2000XL and a Roland VS hardware multitracker, and he came to the SP-303 the same way a lot of people did in the early 2000s: through Madlib and J Dilla.

[Gazillion Industries](https://gazillionindustries.com/) makes plugins for people working this way: a loop, some drums, and one decision about how much to interfere.

## What he sampled

Eighties soul and smooth jazz, cartoon and superhero dialogue, and audio pulled straight off television. Madlib's account of watching him work includes him lifting something from a jazz channel's advertisement. That is the DOOM sample palette in one anecdote: not crate-digging as connoisseurship but a wide, undiscriminating ear that treated a cartoon narrator and a Blue Note record as the same kind of raw material.

The Special Herbs series, released under the Metal Fingers name, is where the instrumental version of that sits, and it is the most useful thing to study if you want to hear the method without the voice on top.

## The writing, which is a production question

Ta-Nehisi Coates watched him work for a New Yorker profile and found the rhyme books were not organized into verses. DOOM described the arranging job as a comedy problem: find whatever would be funny, get as many of those in a row as possible, make them fit. "I liken it to comedy standup."

That explains the density. A DOOM verse is not built to land one point at the end; it is built so something happens every two bars. Which is also why the beats stay simple: a busy, chopped, shifting instrumental underneath that writing would be two people talking at once.

## The masks that were not him

From around 2007 he sent other performers on stage in the mask, and audiences noticed. One documented instance: a London show in March 2010 where a journalist in the room reported the performer was not him. It caused real anger among people who had paid, and it is the logical endpoint of an identity built on a mask rather than a face. He also spent his later years unable to re-enter the United States after travelling to the UK, which is the practical reason a British-born artist who grew up in New York ended up living in England.

## Questions people ask

### When was MF DOOM born?

13 July 1971, in London. The 9 January date that circulated for two decades has been retracted by the outlets that published it.

### What equipment did MF DOOM use?

An Akai MPC-2000XL and a Roland VS hardware multitracker are the machines most consistently named, along with a Casio FZ sampler he had from the early days. Operation: Doomsday was made on a borrowed sampler in somebody else's apartment.

### Did MF DOOM produce his own beats?

Most of them, and a great many for other artists under the name Metal Fingers. The major exception is Madvillainy, produced by Madlib, and the DANGERDOOM record, produced by Danger Mouse.

### How did MF DOOM make his beats?

In his own words: find the loop, put drums to it, polish it with an 808, and keep it as close to the original as possible. He arranged the writing afterward, to the beat.

### When did MF DOOM die?

31 October 2020. His family announced it two months later, on 31 December 2020.

**DOSE 95 at MIX 45** — the squashed copy under the dry one, which is most of how loops like these get their weight.

We make [DRUGS](https://gazillionindustries.com/drugs.html). DOSE 95 at MIX 45 — the squashed copy under the dry one, which is most of how loops like these get their weight.

## What to take from it

Two things, and neither requires a mask. Find loops that are already finished and resist improving them, which is harder than it sounds and is the whole discipline of his beats. And treat arrangement as a separate craft from writing: he wrote lines in isolation and assembled them later, by feel, for maximum hits per bar. Our guide to [flipping a sample](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-flip-a-sample/) is mostly about the opposite instinct, which is exactly why it is worth reading against this.

A group dropped, a brother gone, a decade unaccounted for, and then a catalog built mostly out of records other people had already thrown away.

# The Minimoog Voyager

> The Minimoog Voyager explained: why Bob Moog built it in 2002, what the dual filters and touch surface do, every variant, and what it is good at.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/minimoog-voyager/  
Published 2026-09-20, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries.

---

In 1970 Bob Moog put a synthesizer in a wooden case with a keyboard on it and no patch cables, because working musicians could not carry a wall of modules to a gig. Thirty-two years later, having lost and won back the right to use his own name, he did it again.

The Minimoog Voyager is a monophonic analog synthesizer designed by Robert Moog and released by Moog Music in the summer of 2002, the first new Minimoog since the original Model D went out of production in the early eighties. It keeps the three-oscillator, ladder-filter architecture of the 1970 instrument and adds a second filter, patch memory, MIDI, CV inputs and a touch surface. Production ran for thirteen years and ended in September 2015, after more than 14,000 units: slightly more than the original Minimoog ever sold.

## The short version

- **Released**: summer 2002, designed by Robert Moog

- **Voices**: monophonic, 44 keys with velocity and aftertouch

- **Oscillators**: three, plus noise and an external audio input

- **Filters**: two: dual lowpass, or highpass into lowpass, with spacing

- **Memory**: 128 presets, expandable to 896

- **Discontinued**: September 2015, over 14,000 made

## Why it exists

The original Minimoog was a practical answer to an impractical instrument. Modular systems cost tens of thousands of dollars and had to be patched by hand for every sound, so Moog's engineers hard-wired the most useful connections, bolted on a keyboard and made something a band could put in a van. It ran from 1970 into the early eighties and sold over 12,000 units, which for an instrument that plays one note at a time is a strange kind of triumph.

Then Moog lost the company. The name went with it, and for years he traded as Big Briar, building theremins and effects while other people sold instruments with his surname on them. He got the trademark back and renamed the company Moog Music in 2002, and the Voyager arrived the same year. The first 600 were Signature Editions at $3,495, each one carrying his autograph. Bob Moog died on 21 August 2005, of a brain tumor diagnosed that April, three years into the production run of the instrument that brought his name home.

## What is actually on the panel

Three oscillators with triangle, sawtooth, square and narrow rectangular waves, tunable across a wide range, with oscillator three doubling as a second modulation source. A noise generator and an external input, so you can run other instruments through the filters.

Two filters, which is the biggest musical change from the Model D. In dual lowpass mode you get two ladder filters, one per channel, with a SPACING control that offsets them from each other: a single sound with two different amounts of brightness in it, which in stereo reads as width and in mono as a subtle formant. In highpass-lowpass mode the same pair becomes a band, and spacing sets how wide it is. Two ADSR envelopes, one for the filter and one for the amplifier. An LFO from 0.2 to 50 Hz with triangle, square and two flavors of sample and hold.

Then the modern parts: 128 patch locations expandable to 896, MIDI in, out and through, 14 CV and gate inputs on the back for anyone who wants to treat it as a module again, and a touch surface that reports three values at once from where your finger is and how much of it is touching. The touch surface is the part people either build their playing around or never use twice.

## The variants

- **Signature Edition** (2002): the first 600, $3,495, signed.

- **Standard** (2002 on): $2,995.

- **Anniversary Edition** (2004–05): black cabinet, backlit panel, $3,295.

- **Electric Blue** (2005 on) and the **Select Series** (2006 on), which let buyers specify cabinet and lighting.

- **Rack Mount Edition** (2005): five rack spaces, MIDI controlled, and stackable up to sixteen units for polyphony by brute force.

- **Old School** (2008–09): no memory, no MIDI, no touch surface. A Model D argument in a Voyager case.

- **XL** (2010): 61 keys, a ribbon controller and a patch bay.

- **10th Anniversary Gold** (2012): 31 units, 24-karat gold, $15,000.

## What it is good at

Bass, first. One oscillator an octave down, a second detuned by a few cents against it, the filter low and the envelope doing most of the work: that is a bass line that occupies the whole bottom of a record without a single dB of EQ. Two filters make it more interesting than the usual monosynth bottom, because you can let one of them pass a little more of the harmonics than the other and get bite and weight from the same note.

Leads and hooks, second, especially with the touch surface mapped to filter cutoff, so the phrase moves because your hand moved. And thirdly the thing monosynths are worst at and this one is unusually good at: sitting quietly. Turn the resonance down, open the filters halfway, play chords one note at a time, and it behaves like an instrument in a room rather than a machine making a noise.

There is a hip hop footnote worth having. A Voyager that belonged to [J Dilla](https://gazillionindustries.com/j-dilla/) is in the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture, donated by his mother in 2014 along with his sampler, its power cord, a cable and the factory soft case. The museum's record puts its serial number at 263, inside the first run, and dates it 2002 to 2005. The instrument is not in that case as a synthesizer. It is there as evidence about how a particular producer worked.

**BEEF at 96.** Saturation and loudness, for when a synth needs to stop being polite.

We make [BEEFY](https://gazillionindustries.com/beefy.html). BEEF at 96. Saturation and loudness, for when a synth needs to stop being polite.

## Where it costs you

It plays one note at a time, it is heavy, and it costs more used now than several polyphonic instruments that will do more of the obvious jobs. Analog oscillators drift, so tuning is a habit rather than an event. The patch memory stores panel positions, which means recalling a patch leaves every physical knob pointing at the wrong value until you move it, and that trips people who came from digital instruments. And the touch surface rewards practice in a way that is genuinely off-putting for the first month.

Against all of that: it is one of the few instruments where the difference between a beginner and someone who has lived with it is audible in four notes.

## Questions people ask

### What is special about the Moog Voyager?

It is the Minimoog architecture with a second filter, patch memory, MIDI and CV, designed by Robert Moog himself and built after he regained the rights to his name. The dual filters with their spacing control, and the three-axis touch surface, are the parts you cannot get on the original.

### What are the differences between the Voyager and the original Minimoog?

The Model D of 1970 has one lowpass ladder filter, no patch memory, no MIDI and no CV inputs beyond the basics. The Voyager has two filters with a spacing control, 128 presets expandable to 896, full MIDI, 14 CV and gate inputs, a touch surface, and a velocity- and pressure-sensitive keyboard. The core sound is closely related; the control over it is not.

### Is the Minimoog discontinued?

Voyager production ended in September 2015 after thirteen years. Moog has since reissued the original Model D twice, in 2016 and again in 2022, so a new Minimoog has been available on and off since, but not the Voyager.

### How many Minimoog Voyagers were made?

More than 14,000 across all variants over thirteen years, which is slightly more than the original Minimoog managed in its own production run.

### Is the Voyager polyphonic?

No. It plays one note at a time, with low, high or last-note priority. The Rack Mount Edition could be stacked, up to sixteen units, for people who wanted polyphony badly enough to buy it sixteen times.

Two instruments, thirty-two years apart, built for the same reason: put the thing in a case a person can carry, and let them play it with their hands.

# The creation of the MPC

> How the MPC came to exist: the Linn machines that failed first, what Akai and Roger Linn each contributed, and the swing control in the designer's own words.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/mpc-creation/  
Published 2026-09-20, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries.

---

In February 1986 Roger Linn's company went under, killed by the software in a machine meant to be its future. Two years later the same designer shipped the box that became the standard instrument of hip hop, and the part everyone copies is one percentage field on a menu page.

The Akai MPC60 was released on 8 December 1988 at $5,000, designed by Roger Linn and built by Akai. It put a 12-bit sampler, sixteen velocity-sensitive pads and a MIDI sequencer in one box, with a timing engine running at 96 clock ticks per quarter note and a swing control that delays every second sixteenth note by an amount you choose between 50 and 75 percent. Those two numbers, and the way they interact with what you play, are most of why producers still argue about this machine.

## The short version

- **MPC60**: 8 December 1988, $5,000, 12-bit at 40 kHz

- **MPC3000**: 1994: 16-bit linear at 44.1 kHz, 32 voices, filters

- **Resolution**: 96 ticks per quarter note, on both

- **Swing**: 50% to 75%, delaying every even-numbered sixteenth

- **Linn's settings**: 54% to loosen straight sixteenths, 62% for a relaxed swing

- **Linn leaves**: design involvement ends at the MPC2000 in 1997

## Before Akai

Linn's first machine, the LM-1, was the first drum machine to play samples of real drums. The LinnDrum followed and sold around 5,000 units between 1982 and 1985. Then came the Linn 9000, introduced in 1984 at $5,000, which put a 32-track MIDI sequencer and eighteen pressure-sensitive rubber pads in one instrument. On paper it was everything that came afterward. In practice its software never worked properly, about 1,100 were built, and Linn Electronics closed in February 1986.

That failure is the reason the MPC exists in the form it does. Linn had already designed the instrument; what he needed was a manufacturer with the engineering depth to ship it.

## What each side actually did

Akai built it and Linn designed it, and Linn has been consistent about the split: the concept, the interface, the feel and the timing were his, the hardware engineering and manufacturing were Akai's. The relationship ran through the MPC60, the MPC60 MkII and the MPC3000, and ended when Akai went a different way. In Linn's words: "We collaborated until Akai decided to make their MPC2000 without me in order to avoid my design royalties." That was 1997. The royalty payments themselves continued until 2006, when Numark bought Akai out of bankruptcy. Those are two separate events and most retellings run them together.

## Swing, in the designer's own words

This is the part worth reading twice, because it is the mechanism behind an entire genre's worth of feel and it is not complicated. Linn:

"My implementation of swing has always been very simple: I merely delay the second 16th note within each 8th note. In other words, I delay all the even-numbered 16th notes within the beat (2, 4, 6, 8, etc.)... 50% is no swing, meaning that both 16th notes within each 8th note are given equal timing. And 66% means perfect triplet swing... The fun comes in the in-between settings. For example, a 90 BPM swing groove will feel looser at 62% than at a perfect swing setting of 66%. And for straight 16th-note beats (no swing), a swing setting of 54% will loosen up the feel without it sounding like swing."

The MPC60 manual gives the same two settings as worked examples, both at 100 bpm on sixteenth notes: 54 percent, which "removes the stiffness from perfect 1/16-note timing and is especially useful on drum sequences using 1/16-note hi-hats", and 62 percent, which it describes as "more relaxed than a perfect triplet swing". The control lives on the Timing Correct page and only appears when the note value is set to eighths or sixteenths.

Two practical notes that get lost. The delay is applied to every even sixteenth equally, so swing is a proportion of the note rather than a fixed number of milliseconds, and it scales with tempo automatically. And 96 ticks per quarter note is a coarse grid by modern standards, which is exactly why these machines offer a handful of usable shuffle positions rather than a continuous sweep. The limitation is part of the sound.

[Gazillion Industries](https://gazillionindustries.com/) makes plugins tuned by ear, which is the same argument in a different box: pick the behavior that makes people move, then build the control around it.

## The MPC3000

The 1994 model is the one most associated with the golden era, and the manual's own list of what changed is the best summary anyone has written. Sampling went from 12-bit non-linear at 40 kHz to 16-bit linear at 44.1 kHz, with stereo sampling and a digital input added. Memory went from 2 MB to 16 MB and the five-second per-sound cap disappeared. Voices doubled from 16 to 32, and each got a dynamic lowpass filter with its own envelope and resonance. Sequence memory rose about 30 percent to 75,000 notes. Pad banks went from two to four.

And one addition that matters more than its billing: a Shift Timing feature, independent of timing correction, that moves notes earlier or later by an amount you set. Combined with per-track swing, that is the toolkit behind the rhythmic arguments of the next decade. Our piece on [J Dilla](https://gazillionindustries.com/j-dilla/) goes through what one producer did with it.

What did not change: the sequencer still ran at 96 ticks per quarter note.

## What "turning quantize off" actually means

The story that a producer switched quantize off and played by hand is repeated constantly, and as a description of an approach it is fair. As a technical explanation it is wrong. On these machines, quantize off is a setting called OFF(1/384), and the manual is explicit about what it does: "No timing correction — in this setting, the highest resolution of the MPC60 is used — 96 divisions per 1/4-note." Your notes are not free. They are landing on a 384-per-bar grid, which at 90 bpm puts the ticks about 7 milliseconds apart.

That is fine enough to capture the feel of a hand, and coarse enough that the machine is quietly making decisions for you. Both things are true, and the interesting music came from people who knew it.

## After the MPC3000

The line continued without its designer: the MPC2000 and 2000XL, the 4000, the 1000 and 2500, the 5000, and then the software-and-controller era with the Renaissance, the Live, the X and the One. Whether the later machines feel like the early ones is the longest-running argument in beatmaking forums, and it is partly a question about swing implementations and partly nostalgia for a workflow with no undo.

The pads, though, went everywhere. Sixteen squares in a four-by-four grid, velocity sensitive, one sound each, is now the default physical interface for making rhythm on a computer, and it came from a man trying to ship the machine that had already bankrupted him once.

## Questions people ask

### Who invented the MPC?

Roger Linn designed it and Akai manufactured it. Linn had previously built the LM-1, the LinnDrum and the Linn 9000 under his own company, which closed in February 1986.

### When did the MPC come out and what did it cost?

The MPC60 was released on 8 December 1988 at $5,000. Linn's own account adds that it was later reduced to $3,500.

### What is MPC swing and what does the percentage mean?

It delays every even-numbered sixteenth note within the beat. The number is the share of time given to the first note of each pair: 50 percent is straight, 66 percent is perfect triplet swing, and 75 percent is the maximum. Values between 50 and about 66 are where most of the useful feel lives.

### What swing setting should I use?

The designer's own suggestions are 54 percent to loosen straight sixteenths without it sounding swung, and around 62 percent for a swing that feels more relaxed than a strict triplet. Both assume sixteenth notes; adjust by ear for the track.

### What is the difference between the MPC60 and the MPC3000?

The MPC3000 sampled at 16-bit linear 44.1 kHz instead of 12-bit at 40 kHz, had 16 MB of memory instead of 2, doubled the voices to 32, added a filter per voice, added stereo sampling and a digital input, and added Shift Timing. The sequencer resolution stayed at 96 ticks per quarter note.

## Where it still matters

If you never touch one of these machines, two things from it are still worth stealing. The swing percentages are real numbers you can dial into any DAW, and 54 and 62 are better starting points than the 8 percent your host defaults to. And shifting one voice against another, rather than nudging a whole pattern, is a technique rather than a piece of hardware. See [how to make boom bap drums](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-boom-bap-drums/) and [how to chop a drum break](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-chop-a-drum-break/).

A software failure closed one company and forced the design into someone else's factory. The grid it shipped with is still under most of the rhythm you hear.

# The SP-404 and the sound of Los Angeles

> How Roland's SP-404, a cheap battery-powered sampler seen as a DJ add-on, became the instrument of LA's Low End Theory beat scene and the sound lo-fi grew from.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/sp-404-history/  
Published 2026-09-14, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries.

---

For almost twelve years of Wednesdays, the most important instrument in a sweaty room in Lincoln Heights was a gray box the size of a hardcover book, running on AA batteries. The Airliner had a small bar in the back and a patio with a stairway up to a second stage, and the night held there, Low End Theory, is still spoken of in hushed tones. You had to be there.

Roland released the SP-404 in 2005 as an affordable, battery-powered sampler with a built-in mic and effects, and its engineers later said the public saw it as a DJ add-on. LA's beat scene, centered on Low End Theory, made it a live instrument and a sound: vinyl-sim crunch, resampled loops, effects played like a mixer. That sound fed the beat tapes lo-fi grew from.

## The short version

- **Released**: 2005, unveiled at Summer NAMM

- **Family**: BOSS SP-202 (1998), SP-303 (2001), then Roland's SP-404

- **Why it stuck**: cheap, portable, battery power, effects on anything, resampling

- **Scene**: Low End Theory, Lincoln Heights, 2006 to 2018

- **The sound**: Vinyl Simulator, compression, lo-fi, DJFX Looper

- **Successors**: SP-404SX (2009), SP-404A (2017), SP-404MKII (2021)

## Before the 404: the doctors

The story starts with BOSS, Roland's effects brand, and a little box called the SP-202 Dr. Sample, reviewed in early 1998 as a portable looping sampler for DJs. It already ran on batteries and had a microphone built in. Sound On Sound's reviewer wondered, at the time, whether it might become a cult classic, which is the kind of guess critics make about everything and are almost never right about.

In 2001 the SP-303 followed. It dropped the batteries and the mic, added resampling, and introduced an effect called Vinyl Simulator. That one button would outlive the machine. In 2002, at a Red Bull Music Academy lecture in São Paulo, Madlib held up his SP-303 and called it his main sampler. On the same trip he made beats for what became *Madvillainy* in a hotel room, with a portable record player, the 303 and a borrowed cassette deck. The album came out on March 23, 2004, and it's still the record half the beat scene describes as the moment everything tilted.

The 303 got around. MF DOOM, who rhymed over those beats, came to it through Madlib and J Dilla, and in a late-2004 interview praised its live feel and raw sound. J Dilla kept one at the end: during his long 2005 stay at Cedars-Sinai, friends from Stones Throw brought an SP-303 and a portable 45 player to his bedside, and with the 303 and his MPC he made the beats that became *Donuts*. His hands swelled so badly that his mother, Ma Dukes, massaged them so he could keep working, and House Shoes, his longtime friend from Detroit and an SP user himself, came to see him there. The album was mixed afterward and released on February 7, 2006, his 32nd birthday, three days before he died.

## A box nobody saw coming

Roland unveiled the SP-404 in July 2005: twelve pads, 29 effects, a built-in mic, a CompactFlash slot, and power from six AA batteries. The pitch was simple. Turn it on, aim, record. It kept Vinyl Simulator, and it quietly slipped in an effect called DJFX Looper as number 24 on the list, the kind of detail that ends up defining a scene.

Almost nobody at Roland treated it as a landmark. Years later, Takeo Shirato, the engineer who led the MKII project, said he honestly hadn't expected the 404 to become popular, and that people in 2005 saw it as a supplementary tool for DJs. Kenji Yamada, who designed the original, said he had never imagined a successor would appear. Reverb's history of the machine describes modest early sales and slow adoption. When the SP-404SX arrived in 2009, Roland's launch release pitched it at DJs and engineers triggering jingles. The next 404, in 2017, was that same SX in new colors, positioned as an add-on to a drum machine. **Between the SX and a genuinely new 404, twelve years went by.**

## Los Angeles makes it an instrument

Before Low End Theory there was Sketchbook, a Tuesday night that DJ Kutmah ran at Little Temple. Then in October 2006, Daddy Kev opened Low End Theory at The Airliner in Lincoln Heights with resident DJs DJ Nobody and edIT (D-Styles took edIT's place after the first year). About thirty beat heads showed up that first night, and Daddy Kev insisted on a real sound system from the start. Flying Lotus came around so often that the club's oral history calls him the honorary sixth resident. Within a few years the room had helped launch Flying Lotus, TOKiMONSTA, Nosaj Thing, Daedelus and Thundercat, and it ran more than 600 Wednesdays before closing in August 2018. Around 2010 to 2012 it was touring Japan once or twice a year, carrying the culture of that one room to the other side of the Pacific. Reverb calls it perhaps the single biggest shift in 404 culture. Roland itself says it was one of the first places people could try the 404's effects live.

That's where the box stopped being a sampler and became something you played. Effects weren't set and forgotten; they were ridden, like a DJ riding a filter. Loops were resampled through effects and resampled again until a beat was committed and couldn't be taken back. The limits were the point.

## The people

Ras G made the 404 the center of shows that people still describe in seismic terms. His first trip overseas was played on an SP-303 borrowed from DIBIA$E. Shirato says a Ras G set on a 404SX in Tokyo in 2012 changed the way he thought about the machine. After Ras G died in 2019, his family marked April 4 as Ras G Day, a date the 404 community already considered its own.

DIBIA$E started on an SP-303 next to a drum machine, for the effects and filters the drum machine didn't have, and has talked about running whole beats through a 303 or 404 for its compression, and about how differently the vinyl-sim squash behaves on each. Roland put DIBIA$E in its 2019 short film *Beat Culture & the SP-404* alongside Flying Lotus and Ras G, consulted DIBIA$E while building the MKII, and featured DIBIA$E in its 2026 404 Day livestream.

Samiyam, who found the SP-303 as a teenager in Michigan and whose *Rap Beats Vol. 1* was the first release on Flying Lotus's Brainfeeder label in 2008, held up a 404 in a 2012 video and said, in effect, that everything went in there. Teebs told NPR in 2010 that he recorded everything into his 404, a microwave door included. Kenny Segal, the Los Angeles producer behind billy woods's *Hiding Places* (2019) and *Maps* (2023), told POW in 2020 that he prefers the original 404 to the cleaner SX because the old one has the versions of the effects he likes most, and has played beat sets straight off it. Daedelus, who released *Live at Low End Theory* in 2008, had already made the track "Experience" that Madlib sampled for Madvillain's "Accordion," and years later, teaching at Berklee, was among the faculty already using a 404 before the school launched its SP-404 course.

The room kept making new players. Linafornia grew up in Leimert Park, got a 404 in 2012 and added an SP-555 in 2015, which she has called the 404 on steroids; beat battle wins led to Low End Theory sets and eventually a residency, and Ras G was her friend and peer. She has said women told her they bought a 404 after seeing her play.

Far past that room, the 404 kept finding new hands. Bad Snacks built live sets around it and sat on the judging panel for Roland's SP beat tape contest alongside DIBIA$E and Just Blaze. Sarah, The Illstrumentalist, a Raleigh-born producer, has posted live sets on the 404SX and played the MKII for 404 Day 2023.

## A sound, not just a sampler

The 404 sound is mostly a handful of buttons pushed too far. Vinyl Simulator, born on the 303, gives drums a squashed, dusty density. Compression glues a loop into a single block. DJFX Looper stutters and reverses on command. When Roland made LO-FI a proper effect on the SX, it said the reason was that customers liked the lo-fi sound of the 303. Roland's own engineers describe producers chaining a 404SX into an SP-303 just to get both machines' effects at once. The instrument's tone came from its users refusing to give up the older box.

## The genre it fed

Careful here, because this is where the myths live. Roland says the 404 helped usher in lo-fi hip hop. Sound On Sound calls it popular in the lo-fi scene and traces that scene's influences to SP users like Dilla and Madvillain. But the big mainstream stories about the lo-fi YouTube streams don't mention the sampler at all, and they credit Dilla, Nujabes and *Madvillainy*. The fair version: the SP line shaped the beat-tape sound that lo-fi grew out of, and two of the records lo-fi producers name first, *Madvillainy* and *Donuts*, were built with SP-303s close at hand.

## Roland comes back

In October 2021 Roland announced the SP-404MKII at $499.99, and this time it came from the community. Shirato says he went through almost every SP post online, asked producers including Flying Lotus, DIBIA$E and Just Blaze for feedback, and brought back the SP-303's Vinyl Simulator on purpose, alongside new Lo-fi and Cassette Simulator effects. He framed the machine as a way of returning a favor. Roland now celebrates 404 Day every April 4; for the 404's twentieth anniversary in 2025 it held events in more than fifteen cities, and Berklee's first SP-404MKII course filled up immediately.

**4 bit at 8 kHz.** Bits make it grainy; the sample rate is what makes it clang.

We make [F(ilter)12](https://gazillionindustries.com/f12.html). 4 bit at 8 kHz. Bits make it grainy; the sample rate is what makes it clang.

## Why a plugin company cares

Because every Gazillion plugin started with a sound from these boxes and a set of ears raised on it. None of them are copies, and nothing in them was measured from hardware; they're tuned by ear, chasing a feeling. DRUGS chases the squash that Vinyl Simulator put on a break. F(ilter)12 chases what the 404's lo-fi does to a sample. TRIPLE OG chases the cassette sim on the newest machine. SKRUU chases the pitch knob on the little Dr. Sample where the whole line began. If you've never used an SP, they're a way in. If you have, you'll know what we were listening for.

## SP404 or SP-404, and the effect people are looking for

It gets written both ways, and a search for one misses much of what exists about the other. Worth knowing if you are reading around the subject rather than just reading this.

More useful: most people arriving at this name are not looking for the hardware at all. They are looking for one effect off it — the lo-fi setting — because they heard it on a record and had no word for it. That effect is a process rather than a machine, it is several things happening at once rather than one, and it is reproducible. It has its own guide in [how to make lofi beats](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-lofi-beats/).

## Questions people ask

### What is the SP-404?

A compact, battery-powered sampler Roland released in 2005, with pads, a built-in mic and a bank of effects. It became a central instrument in Los Angeles's beat scene and in instrumental and lo-fi hip hop.

### When did the SP-404 come out?

The original SP-404 was unveiled in July 2005. The SP-404SX followed in 2009, the SP-404A in 2017, and the SP-404MKII was announced in October 2021.

### Why is the SP-404 so popular?

It's affordable, portable and self-contained, its effects work on anything you feed them, and its resampling workflow pushes you to commit to ideas. Low End Theory turned it into a live instrument, and a generation of producers built their sound on it.

### What's the difference between the SP-404 and the SP-404MKII?

The MKII adds velocity-sensitive pads, a screen, far more storage and many more effects, while keeping battery power and classic effects like Vinyl Simulator and DJFX Looper. Roland designed it from years of user community requests.

The Airliner's Wednesdays ended in 2018, and the room can't be rebuilt. The gray boxes are still out there, on folding tables everywhere, running on batteries, doing things nobody who built them imagined.

# Best detune plugins

> How detune plugins work, what separates a good one from a bad one, free and paid picks verified today, and how to set detune on guitars.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/best-detune-plugins/  
Published 2026-09-24, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries, who make SKRUU.

---

Two guitar takes, hard panned, and on the monitors the part sounded like a wall. In the car it folded into one thin line up the middle. Same file, same mix.

A detune plugin plays a copy of your signal at a slightly different pitch and mixes it back in. Pitch offsets are measured in cents, and 100 cents is one semitone; useful detune lives between about 3 and 20 cents, where the ear hears two players instead of one bad note. The one to reach for is a micro pitch shifter with an independent cent offset per voice and a dry path it leaves alone. Free ones do the same job. All of them have to be checked in mono.

## The short version

- **What**: a copy of the signal at a small pitch offset, mixed back in

- **Unit**: cents — 100 cents is a semitone, 1200 is an octave

- **Range**: 3–20 cents for width; past 25 it reads as out of tune

- **Why it widens**: left and right no longer match, so the ear counts two sources

- **The catch**: mono sums lose most of it and can comb the midrange

- **Free and good**: Kilohearts Essentials, MAutoPitch, Blue Cat's Chorus

**A small offset up.** Detune is the same control as pitch shift, kept tiny.

## What detune does to the signal

Two copies of the same note at slightly different pitches beat against each other. The beat rate is the difference between the two frequencies, so it is not a fixed wobble across the spectrum: it scales with pitch. Offset a 220 Hz note by 5 cents and the copy lands at 220.64 Hz, a beat of 0.64 Hz, which is one pulse every 1.6 seconds. The same 5 cents on a 2 kHz partial gives a beat near 5.8 Hz.

That single fact explains most of what detune sounds like. The top shimmers, the bottom lurches. It is why a detuned pad glitters and a detuned bass sounds seasick, and why the standing advice to high-pass the detuned copy is arithmetic rather than fussiness. Roll the wet voice off below about 150 Hz and the seasick part goes with it.

Add a few milliseconds of delay to the detuned voice and the ear stops hearing a pitch relationship and starts hearing a second performer standing apart. Under about 30 ms the two fuse into one wider source; past 50 ms you hear a distinct double.

## Three ways a plugin gets there

Every detune plugin picks one of three mechanisms, and the mechanism decides what it is good for.

**A modulated delay line.** Chorus, ensemble and vibrato units vary a short delay over time, and a delay whose length is changing produces a pitch offset while it moves. Artifacts are close to nil, because nothing is invented — it is the same sample data read at a drifting rate. The trade is that the offset can never sit still: stop the modulation and the detune stops with it.

**A true pitch shifter.** A granular or spectral engine holds a fixed offset indefinitely: 7 cents up stays 7 cents up. This is what people usually mean by a detune plugin. It costs latency and transient accuracy, because the engine is splicing or resynthesizing, and at small offsets those splices are inaudible on most material and very audible on a dry hi-hat.

**Resampling.** Play the audio faster or slower and the pitch follows, the mechanism described in [what varispeed is](https://gazillionindustries.com/what-is-varispeed/). The offset is exact and there is no algorithm to hear, but length changes with pitch, so a 10-cent copy of a four-minute track drifts about 1.4 seconds by the end. Good for a whole part, wrong for a live insert unless the plugin buffers it back.

A fourth thing sold in the same aisle is not detune at all: pseudo stereo wideners use all-pass phase tricks rather than pitch, so they widen without beating. Keep the two apart in your head.

**The other direction.** Down and up on two copies is the whole trick.

## What separates a good detune plugin from a bad one

Everything in the category sounds broadly fine at 8 cents on a pad. The differences show up on the edges.

- **Independent offsets per voice.** One symmetric knob that spreads both sides equally is a preset with a handle on it. You want the left voice and the right voice set separately, because material is rarely symmetric.

- **Resolution of one cent or finer.** Coarse steps force a choice between too little and too much, and the useful vocal settings sit between 4 and 9 cents.

- **A dry path that is left alone.** Some plugins run the dry signal through the engine to keep it time-aligned, which spends artifacts on the part you wanted untouched. Set mix to zero and null-test against the bypass.

- **Honest latency reporting.** A shifter with a long window that fails to report its delay to the host will smear every parallel path in the session.

- **Per-voice delay in milliseconds.** Time, rather than pitch, is what turns width into a double, and you want that on a control rather than by accident.

[SKRUU](https://gazillionindustries.com/skruu.html) detunes by moving playback speed rather than by splicing grains, so small PITCH offsets have no algorithm to hear, and ELASTIC lets the offset spring back on its own. There's a demo on the page.

## How to test a detune plugin in ten minutes

- Load the plugin on a dry mono source: one guitar take, one vocal, no reverb.

- Set the wet level to unity and the offset to 7 cents up on one side, 7 cents down on the other.

- Listen in stereo for ten seconds, then sum to mono and listen again.

- Measure the drop: if the mono sum loses more than a few dB of level, the two voices are canceling and the setting is too wide.

- High-pass the wet voices at 150 Hz and repeat the mono check.

- Set the mix to zero and null-test the output against the bypassed plugin.

- Run a dry closed hi-hat through it at the same settings and listen for doubled or softened attacks.

- Check the reported latency in the host, then bounce and confirm the bounce lines up with the original.

- Play the bounce on a phone speaker before you keep the setting.

Step nine is the one people skip. A phone speaker is close to mono, rolls the bottom off hard, and is where most of the audience hears the record. If the guitars still sound like two guitars there, the detune is doing real work.

## Where detune goes in the chain

Put it after anything that changes dynamics and before anything that adds space. Compression ahead keeps the two voices at a steady relative level; reverb after puts both copies in one room, which is what sells them as a single performance. Detune into a reverb sounds like a wide instrument; reverb into a detune sounds like a wide room.

On a bus, run it parallel rather than in series, because a send can be EQ'd and a wet/dry knob cannot. High-pass the send at 150 Hz and shelve the top down a couple of dB, and the width arrives without the glitter.

Never detune the low fundamental of a bass. Below roughly 120 Hz the beat period is long enough to read as an unsteady note rather than as width. Split the band and detune only the top.

## Named options, and what each one actually is

Facts below come from each maker's own product page, read today.

**Eventide MicroPitch** is listed at $99 and described as a dual-voiced, fine-resolution pitch shifter for subtle tone fattening, with delays on board for slap back effects. It runs as AAX, VST2 and VST3 on Windows 10 and later, and as AAX, AU, VST2 and VST3 on macOS 10.14 and later on Intel and Apple Silicon, plus AUv3 and standalone on iOS. Two voices, each with its own pitch and delay, is the control set described above.

**Waves Doubler** is described on its page as a four-voice doubler and imager with modulation and detuning — more voices than most parts need and more than most plugins offer. The price on that page is injected by script and did not load, so check it yourself.

**Soundtoys Little AlterBoy** is a monophonic voice tool: pitch shifting, formant shifting, a hard-tune mode, MIDI control of the pitch, and a tube drive stage carried over from the same maker's saturation plugin. It aims at vocals rather than width, and the formant control is the reason to keep it in mind — see [formant shifting](https://gazillionindustries.com/formant-shifting/).

## Best free detune plugin

Three free options cover the category between them, and none of them is a demo.

**Kilohearts Essentials** is a bundle of 34 effects, free with an account, and the list includes Pitch Shifter, Chorus, Ensemble, Flanger, Haas, Stereo and Frequency Shifter. Pitch Shifter is the fixed-offset engine, Ensemble and Chorus are the modulated-delay route, Haas is the time-offset route. Three mechanisms in one free download is the fastest way to learn which one your material wants.

**MeldaProduction MAutoPitch** is free, arrives in the MFreeFXBundle, and is built as an automatic tuning plugin for vocals and other monophonic sources, with formant shift and stereo expansion alongside the tuning. If the detune problem is really a backing-vocal problem, start here.

**Blue Cat's Chorus** is freeware: a single-voice chorus with a stereo spread control and a choice of sine or triangle LFO, in most plugin formats for Mac and Windows. The cheapest way to hear what a modulated delay does that a fixed offset cannot.

When the mono check keeps failing, **Polyverse Wider** is a free pseudo-stereo widener that increases the image of a mono signal by up to 200% and stays in phase with itself when summed, in VST2, VST3, AU and AAX for 64-bit Windows and macOS 10.9 and later. Different mechanism, same job, no beating.

**TIME moved, PITCH held.** Length and pitch on separate knobs.

## Best guitar detune plugin, and how to set it

Guitars are why this search term exists. A rhythm part tracked once and copied to both sides is identical left and right, so it collapses to the center, and a few cents of offset on each copy pushes it back out. The tool is a two-voice micro shifter with per-side cent control; the free stand-in is the Kilohearts Pitch Shifter on two channels.

- Duplicate the guitar track and hard-pan the two copies.

- Insert the detune plugin on each copy, not on the bus.

- Set the left copy to 6 cents down and the right copy to 6 cents up.

- Add 12 ms of delay to one side and 18 ms to the other.

- High-pass both detuned copies at 150 Hz.

- Sum to mono and pull the offsets back until the mono level stops dropping.

- Return to stereo and set the final wet level by ear against the drums.

Two other guitar jobs get called detune and are something else. Dropping a recorded part a semitone is a shift of exactly 100 cents, a whole step is 200, and that wants a plugin built for range rather than width — the method is in [how to change pitch without changing tempo](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-change-pitch-without-changing-tempo/). Fixing a note that drifted sharp inside a chord is tuning work, and no amount of width hides it.

## What it costs you

Detune buys width and spends three things. It spends mono, always: two signals that differ cannot sum without interference, and the arithmetic of [phase cancellation](https://gazillionindustries.com/phase-cancellation/) does not negotiate. It spends definition, because a smeared attack is the price of two attacks a few milliseconds apart. And on a clear melodic line it spends pitch certainty — a lead vocal detuned past about 12 cents starts to sound like a singer who nearly got there.

So use it sparingly and late. Get the part right, get it in tune, get it sitting, add width last, and check [mono compatibility](https://gazillionindustries.com/mono-compatibility/) before you commit.

## Questions people ask

### What is the best detune plugin?

For most people it is a two-voice micro pitch shifter with an independent cent offset and delay per voice. Eventide MicroPitch is listed at $99 and is described by its maker as exactly that: a dual-voiced, fine-resolution pitch shifter with delays. If you need four voices rather than two, Waves Doubler is described as a four-voice doubler and imager with modulation and detuning.

### What is the best free detune plugin?

Kilohearts Essentials, which is free with an account and includes Pitch Shifter, Chorus, Ensemble and Haas among its 34 effects, so you get all three detune mechanisms in one download. MeldaProduction MAutoPitch is free and better suited to vocals, and Blue Cat's Chorus is freeware with a stereo spread control if you want the modulated-delay flavor.

### What is the best guitar detune plugin?

The same two-voice micro shifter, used on two hard-panned copies rather than on the bus, with roughly 6 cents of offset each way and 12 to 18 ms of delay. Set it per copy, high-pass the wet voices at 150 Hz, and check the mono sum before you keep it.

### How many cents should I detune?

Start at 7 and move from there. Below 3 cents the effect is nearly inaudible on most material; above about 20 cents the ear stops hearing width and starts hearing an out-of-tune second voice. Pads take more than vocals, and low instruments take less than high ones, because the beat rate scales with frequency.

Two copies, one sent up and one sent down, and the width is built out of speed.

**SAMPLING GRADE at LO-FI 1.** 7.81 kHz rather than 31.25.
